title: Insert into a Sorted Circular Linked List
statement:
You get `head`, some node of a circular singly linked list (the last node's `next` leads back to the first), and an integer `insertVal`. Read around the circle from the right starting node, the values are in non-decreasing order, but `head` can be any node, not necessarily the one holding the smallest value. Add one new node holding `insertVal` so that the circle is still sorted in the same sense; when several spots work, any of them is accepted. Keep every existing node and its order.

- If `head` is `null` (the list is empty), make a circle of one new node that points to itself and return that node.
- Otherwise return `head`, the node you were given.

Nodes are `ListNode` objects with `val` and `next`; create the new one with `new ListNode(insertVal)`. Each case is written as `[head, insertVal]`, where `head` lists the values met when walking once around the circle starting at the given node (`[]` when empty). The result is shown the same way, starting at the node you return.
constraints: The list has between 0 and 5 * 10^4 nodes
Walking around the circle from some node gives non-decreasing values
notes:
## Intuition

A sorted circle has at most one place where the values drop, from the largest value back to the smallest. The new value fits either between two neighbours that bracket it (`prev.val <= insertVal <= curr.val`), or at that drop when it is a new maximum or a new minimum. Walking once around the circle from `head` with a pair of pointers finds such a spot. If a whole lap finds none, every value is equal, and any spot works.

## Approach

1. Make the new node. If `head` is `null`, point it at itself and return it.
2. Start `prev = head` and `curr = head.next`.
3. Stop when `insertVal` lies between `prev.val` and `curr.val`.
4. Also stop at the drop (`prev.val > curr.val`) when `insertVal` is at least the maximum or at most the minimum.
5. Otherwise step both pointers forward; quit after one full lap.
6. Link `prev -> node -> curr` and return `head`.

## Example 1, step by step

The circle is `3 -> 4 -> 1 -> 3` and `insertVal = 2`.

- `prev = 3`, `curr = 4`: 2 is not between them and this is not the drop.
- `prev = 4`, `curr = 1`: this is the drop, but 2 is neither `>= 4` nor `<= 1`.
- `prev = 1`, `curr = 3`: `1 <= 2 <= 3`, so stop.

Linking gives `3 -> 4 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3`, read from `head` as `[3, 4, 1, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): at most one lap around the circle.
- Space: O(1): two pointers and the new node.

## Pitfalls

- Use a `do ... while` (or a step count) so a one-node circle, where `curr === prev`, still runs the checks once and the loop ends.
- When all values are equal and `insertVal` differs, neither condition ever holds; after one lap, insert anywhere instead of looping forever.
- At the drop, accept both a new maximum (`>= prev.val`) and a new minimum (`<= curr.val`).
- Return the original `head`, not the new node, unless the list was empty.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `node` | the new node holding `insertVal` |
| `prev` | the node the new one may follow |
| `curr` | `prev.next`, the node the new one may precede |
